a01.title: Context engineering: what the model sees

beats.say: Your agent did great for ten steps, then started forgetting the task and repeating itself. The model did not get worse. Its context did.

Every turn, the model only sees what you put in its window: instructions, tool results, history. Dump a 20,000 line log into it and the important lines are buried, the bill goes up, and older instructions get pushed out or ignored.
Context engineering means choosing what goes in: summarise old turns, return only the 30 relevant log lines from a tool, and keep the goal and rules pinned at the top.

check.q: An agent gets worse after many steps. What do you fix first?
opts: What goes into its context each turn
check.why: Bloated context hides the goal and the key facts; trim tool output and summarise history.

work: Make tools return a short, structured result instead of raw dumps
Log tokens per turn and alert when context grows past a budget

a02.title: Graders that do not lie

beats.say: Your agent scores 95 percent on your evals, then fails on real tickets. Often the grader is the problem, not the agent.
A grader that checks for keywords passes an answer that mentions the right table but gives the wrong number. A model grader asked is this good tends to say yes, especially to long, confident answers.
Honest graders check the outcome: run the SQL and compare the result, give the model grader a rubric with failing examples, and check the grader itself on cases you labelled by hand.

items: Check the result, not the wording
Test the grader against human labels

check.q: What is the strongest grader for a text-to-SQL agent?
opts: Check the SQL mentions the right tables
Run the SQL and compare its result with the expected result
Ask a model if the SQL looks good
check.why: Execution checks the outcome, which keywords and impressions cannot.

work: Label 20 real cases by hand and measure how often your grader agrees
Prefer executable checks wherever the task has a checkable result

a03.title: When one agent becomes many

beats.say: Splitting work across several agents sounds powerful. It also multiplies cost and creates new ways to fail. When is it worth it?

show.sub: only when the work splits cleanly

beats.say: It pays off when sub-tasks are independent and each needs a lot of its own reading, like checking ten pipelines in parallel. A coordinator gives each worker a narrow brief and gets back a short summary, so no single context fills up.
It fails when the parts depend on each other: workers redo each other's work or contradict. Then one agent with good tools is cheaper and more reliable.

check.q: When does a multi-agent design beat one agent?
opts: When sub-tasks are independent and each needs lots of its own context
check.why: Parallel independent work with separate contexts is the case it is built for.

work: Start with one agent and split only when context or time limits bite
Give each worker a narrow brief and ask for a short structured summary

a04.title: Semantic layers: one definition of revenue

beats.say: Ask an LLM for last month's revenue and it writes perfect SQL that returns the wrong number. Gross or net? Refunds? Which currency? The SQL was fine; the definition was missing.

A semantic layer writes the business definitions down once: revenue is net of refunds, in rupees, by trip date. Dashboards, notebooks and the LLM all ask the layer for revenue instead of writing their own formula.
For text to SQL this is the biggest accuracy win: the model chooses metrics and filters; the layer supplies the logic.

check.q: Why does a semantic layer improve text-to-SQL accuracy?
opts: The model reuses governed metric definitions instead of inventing formulas
check.why: Most wrong answers come from wrong definitions, not wrong syntax.

work: Define your top 10 metrics in a semantic layer before building an AI SQL assistant
Test the assistant on questions with known answers

a05.title: Chunking: where most RAG systems fail

beats.say: Your RAG assistant answers from the wrong runbook, or from half a step. Usually the model is fine. The way the documents were cut up is not.

Retrieval finds chunks whose embeddings are close to the question. Chunks too big blur several topics into one vector, so nothing matches sharply. Chunks too small lose the context that makes a step make sense.
Split on the document's own structure, add a small overlap, and keep the title and section as text in every chunk. Then measure retrieval with real questions before tuning the model.

check.q: Why do very large chunks hurt retrieval?
opts: One vector mixes several topics, so no topic matches strongly
check.why: Embedding a long mixed passage averages its meanings.

work: Build a set of 30 real questions with the right chunk for each
Track retrieval recall before changing the generation prompt

d01.title: Write skew: both checks pass, the rule breaks

beats.say: Two on-call engineers each check that at least one other person is on call, and both go off call at the same moment. Each check was true. Now nobody is on call.
This is write skew. Each transaction read a snapshot, saw two people on call, and updated a different row, its own. Snapshot isolation only stops two writes to the same row, so it lets this through.
Fixes: run at serializable isolation and retry on failure, or lock the rows you checked with select for update, or turn the rule into a constraint.

items: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on what you read

check.q: Why does snapshot isolation allow write skew?
opts: The two transactions update different rows, so no write conflict is detected
check.why: The rule spans rows that neither transaction locked.

work: Look for business rules that read several rows and update one
Protect them with serializable isolation or explicit row locks

j01.title: The JVM under your Spark job

beats.say: Your Spark executors freeze for twenty seconds at a time, and tasks time out. The code did not change. The garbage collector is cleaning up a heap full of objects.

Spark runs on the Java virtual machine. Objects live on a heap, and the garbage collector periodically finds and frees the dead ones. A huge heap with millions of small objects means long pauses, and during a full pause the executor does nothing.

items: Big heap, many objects: long pauses

beats.say: Spark avoids this with off-heap binary data in DataFrames, which is one reason they beat RDDs of Python objects. Check GC time in the Spark UI; above about ten percent, act.

items: Use DataFrames, not RDDs of objects
Watch GC time in the UI

check.q: Why are DataFrames kinder to the garbage collector than RDDs of objects?
opts: They store rows in compact binary form instead of millions of objects
check.why: Fewer objects means less for the collector to scan.

work: Check the GC time column in the Spark UI for slow stages
Prefer several moderate executors over a few giant heaps

m01.title: Slowly changing dimensions, type 2

beats.say: A driver moves from Pune to Bengaluru. Last year's Pune revenue suddenly drops, because every old trip now joins to Bengaluru. Nobody changed the trips.
Overwriting the city is type 1: history is lost. Type 2 keeps history. Close the old row with an end date, and insert a new row with a new surrogate key, the new city and a start date.

show.text:
driver_sk  driver_id  city       valid_from  valid_to
101        D7         Pune       2024-01-01  2026-03-31
245        D7         Bengaluru  2026-04-01  9999-12-31

beats.say: Facts store the surrogate key that was current when the trip happened, so old trips keep Pune and new ones get Bengaluru.

items: Insert a new row, new key
Facts point at the key of their time

check.q: In type 2, how does an old trip keep the old city?
opts: The trip stores the city name
The trip stores the surrogate key that was current at trip time
check.why: Each version has its own key, and facts are joined on that key.

work: Decide per attribute whether history matters (type 2) or not (type 1)
Test that every natural key has exactly one current row

m02.title: Date lists: a month of activity in one number

beats.say: Counting monthly active users by scanning 30 days of events every night is slow and expensive. What if one row per user already knew which days they were active?
A date list stores activity as bits: one bit per day, 1 if the user was active. Each night you shift yesterday's number by one and add today's bit. Thirty days of history fit in one integer.
Then active in the last 7 days is a single bit mask, no scan. Rows drop from users times days to just users.

show.unit: rows read for a monthly active count

check.q: How is the date list updated each night?
opts: Shift the previous value and add today's bit
check.why: It is cumulative: yesterday's state plus one new bit.

work: Build a cumulative table for any metric computed over a rolling window
Store activity as bits when you need many "active in last N days" metrics

m03.title: Data Vault: model for change, not for queries

beats.say: Your company has twelve source systems, and they change every quarter. A star schema in the cleaned layer breaks every time. Data Vault is built for that churn.

It splits data three ways. Hubs hold business keys, like customer id. Links hold relationships, like customer placed order. Satellites hold the descriptive attributes with load dates, one per source. A new source adds a satellite and changes nothing else.
The price: many joins. So you build stars on top for analysts, and keep the vault as the auditable record.

check.q: A new source system arrives. What changes in a Data Vault?
opts: You add a satellite (and links if needed); existing tables stay
check.why: Additive change is the point of the vault.

work: Use a vault in the integration layer when sources change often
Serve analysts from stars or wide tables built on top

p01.title: Why did my list change by itself?

beats.say: Here is a bug almost everyone hits. You pass a list into a function, the function appends to it, and your own list changed. You never touched it. Why?
Because a Python variable is a name tag, not a box. b equals a does not copy the list. It puts a second tag on the same list. So when b appends, a sees it too. There is only one list.

show.text:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # second tag, same list
b.append(4)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]

beats.say: Lists, dicts and sets can change in place. Ints, strings and tuples cannot: changing them makes a new object. Need your own list? Call copy. A shallow copy still shares the dicts inside.

items: a.copy() is shallow; copy.deepcopy copies all

check.q: a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4). What is a now?
check.why: b = a gives the same list a second name, so the append is visible through both.

work: Do not change a list or dict passed into your function unless that is its job; return a new one
Copy shared config before editing it: dict(defaults), or copy.deepcopy for nested data
Use "is" only to test for None

p01.title: Why is pop(0) slow on a big list?

beats.say: Two lines look the same: pop from the end, and pop from the front. On a million items, one is instant and the other moves a million things. Which, and why?

A list is one row of slots in memory, side by side. Adding or removing at the end touches one slot. Removing at the front leaves a hole, so every other item shifts left by one. A million items means a million moves, every time.
So treat a list as fast at the end and slow at the front. For a queue, use a deque, which is fast at both ends. And remember that slicing copies.

check.q: Which of these is O(n) on a list of n items?
check.why: Removing the first item shifts every other item one place left.

work: Use collections.deque for queues and buffers
Never call pop(0) or insert(0, x) in a loop over big data
Remember xs[a:b] makes a copy

p01.title: How is "x in a set" instant?

beats.say: Checking whether an id is in a list of a million ids can take a million comparisons. Checking a set takes about one. Same question, very different cost. What does the set know?

A set turns the value into a number called a hash, and that number says exactly which slot to look in. Like knowing your locker number instead of opening every locker. Dicts work the same way for keys.
That is also why keys must not change: a list cannot be a dict key, because its hash would change after it was stored.

items: Lookup, add, delete: O(1) on average
Keys must be hashable: str, int, tuple
x in something inside a loop? Make it a set

check.q: Why can a list not be a dict key?
opts: A list can change, so its hash would change after it is stored
check.why: The slot is chosen from the hash when the key is stored. If the key could change, the lookup would go to the wrong slot.

work: Inside any loop, check membership against a set or dict, never a list
Group rows with a dict keyed by the grouping column
Use d.get(k, default) instead of catching KeyError

p01.title: 100,000 rows took three hours. Why?

beats.say: A script checks each of 100,000 trips against a list of 100,000 driver ids. It takes hours. The code looks innocent: one loop, one "in".

show.text:
for t in trips:              # n times
    if t["driver"] in ids:   # ids is a list: n more

beats.say: But "in" on a list is itself a loop. A loop inside a loop is n times n: ten billion steps. Make ids a set and each check is one step, so the whole job is a hundred thousand steps.

items: ids as a list: n x n

beats.say: In an interview, say the cost before you run: this is n squared because of the nested scan; a set makes it linear time and linear extra memory.

check.q: trips has n rows and ids is a list of m ids. What does the loop cost?
check.why: Each of the n checks scans up to m ids. With a set it becomes O(n).

work: Before running a job on full data, say its Big-O out loud
Turn nested scans into a set or dict lookup
Time it on 1% of the data first and multiply

p01.title: Four tools that replace ten lines each

beats.say: The collections module has four tools data engineers use every day. Think of them as SQL inside Python.
Counter counts things, like group by with count star, and most common gives the top N. Defaultdict of list groups rows by a key without checking whether the key exists.

show.text:
Counter(cities).most_common(3)   # top 3
groups = defaultdict(list)
groups[t["city"]].append(t)       # group rows

beats.say: Deque with a max length keeps only the newest items: a sliding window. It is also the right queue, fast at both ends. Namedtuple gives a tuple field names, so row dot fare reads like a record.

check.q: You need the last 100 events of a stream, dropping older ones automatically. Which tool?
check.why: A deque with maxlen drops the oldest item each time a new one is added.

work: Top-N report: Counter(...).most_common(n)
Grouping rows in memory: defaultdict(list)
Rolling windows and queues: deque

p01.title: Your script dies on a 20 GB log

beats.say: A script works on a test file and dies with an out of memory error on the real 20 gigabyte log. One line is usually to blame: reading the whole file at once.

show.text:
data = f.read()        # all 20 GB into memory
for line in f:         # one line at a time

beats.say: f dot read loads every byte into memory. Looping over the file reads one line, processes it, and lets it go, so memory stays flat whatever the size. The with block closes the file even if something fails.
Strings cannot change, so plus equals in a loop builds a new string every time. Collect the parts in a list and join once at the end.

check.q: Which keeps memory flat on a huge file?
check.why: Iterating over the file object reads one line at a time.

work: Stream big inputs; never read() a file whose size you do not control
Build output with a list and join
Open files with "with" and an explicit encoding

p01.title: Should we rewrite it in Scala?

beats.say: Your nightly Python job is slow, and the team wants to rewrite it in Scala. An architect asks one question first: where does the time actually go?

show.sub: first: where does the time go?

beats.say: Usually it is a row by row Python loop, or Python functions called on every row inside Spark. Fix that first: use Spark built in functions, SQL, or a vectorised library like Polars or DuckDB.

items: Row loops: vectorise or push to SQL

beats.say: A rewrite costs a second language, hiring and tooling. It is worth it only when Python itself is the limit after those fixes, like a long running stream with large state.

check.q: A slow nightly Python job: what do you check before agreeing to a rewrite?
opts: Where the time goes: row loops, UDFs, waiting on I/O
How many lines the job has
check.why: Most slow Python jobs are slow in one fixable place. Measure before you rewrite.

work: Profile a slow job before proposing a rewrite
Replace Python UDFs in Spark with built-in functions
Write down the condition that would justify another language

p01.title: Why is a Python loop slow but NumPy fast?

beats.say: Summing a million numbers in a Python loop takes about a hundred times longer than numpy dot sum on the same numbers. Same algorithm. Why?

In plain Python every number is a full object somewhere in memory, with a type and a counter. Each plus means looking up the type and making a new object. NumPy keeps raw numbers side by side and runs one compiled loop over them, so each step is a single machine instruction.

items: Python: a box per number, checked every step
NumPy, Polars: raw values in one block

check.q: Why is the Python loop slower?
opts: Each number is a separate object, checked and created step by step
check.why: The work per element is what differs: objects and type checks in Python, raw values in a compiled loop in NumPy.

work: For numeric work over many rows, use NumPy, Polars, DuckDB or Spark built-ins
Keep Python for control flow, APIs and glue

p02.title: A function is just a value

beats.say: Here is a trick that removes whole if-else ladders from pipeline code. In Python, a function is a value, like a number or a string. You can put it in a variable, a list or a dict.

show.sub: store them, pass them, return them

beats.say: So instead of ten if statements that clean each column, keep a dict from column name to cleaning function. Look up the column, call what you find. Adding a column means adding one line, not another branch.

show.text:
rules = {"city": str.title, "fare": float}
clean = {k: rules[k](v) for k, v in row.items()}

beats.say: You already use this every day: sorted with a key, map, and every Spark column function you pass to withColumn.

check.q: f = to_upper (no brackets). What is f?
opts: The function itself, ready to call later
check.why: Without brackets you refer to the function object; with brackets you call it.

work: Replace long if-else chains on column names with a dict of functions
Pass behaviour in as a function instead of a flag when a step needs to vary

p02.title: The default list that remembers

beats.say: A function adds a row to a batch and returns it. Call it once: one row. Call it again with a different row: two rows, including the one from the first call. Nobody passed the old list in. Where did it come from?

show.text:
def add_row(row, batch=[]):
    batch.append(row)
    return batch
add_row(1)   # [1]
add_row(2)   # [1, 2]  ?!

beats.say: Default values are made once, when Python reads the def line, not each time you call. So every call shares the same empty list, and it fills up. The fix: default to None, and create a new list inside the function.
And for flags, put them after a star so callers must name them: overwrite equals true, not a bare true.

items: Never use [] or {} as a default

check.q: When is a default argument value created?
opts: Once, when the function is defined
Only if the caller leaves it out
check.why: That is why a mutable default is shared by every call.

work: Search your codebase for "=[]" and "={}" in function definitions
Make boolean options keyword-only with a bare *

p02.title: Closures: functions that remember

beats.say: You need a retry policy configured once, three tries and two seconds apart, and then used everywhere. You could write a class. Or you could use a closure.

A function defined inside another function can read the outer variables, and it keeps them alive after the outer function has returned. So make multiplier of two returns a function that still remembers two.
To change an outer variable, not just read it, mark it nonlocal. Otherwise Python treats it as a new local and fails. Decorators are built from exactly this.

check.q: Inside a nested function you write n += 1 on an outer n without nonlocal. What happens?
opts: The outer n goes up by one
A new global n is created
check.why: Assignment makes n local to the inner function, and it is read before it has a value.

work: Use a small factory function for configurable helpers such as retry and rate limiting
Mark shared counters nonlocal, or use a class when the state grows

p02.title: Comprehensions are SQL in one line

beats.say: Read a list comprehension left to right like a SQL query: select this expression, from this iterable, where this condition holds. Once you see that, they stop looking cryptic.

show.text:
[t["fare"] for t in trips if t["status"] == "completed"]
#  SELECT fare FROM trips WHERE status = completed

beats.say: They come as lists, dicts and sets. And a version with round brackets, a generator, makes values one at a time, so summing a million fares never builds a million-item list in memory.

items: sum(x for x in ...) builds no list
Faster than a for loop with append

beats.say: Stop when they stop being clear: two for clauses at most, and never use one just for side effects like printing.

show.sub: three nested fors? write a loop

check.q: Which keeps memory flat when summing a million fares?
check.why: Without square brackets it is a generator: one value at a time.

work: Turn append-in-a-loop into a comprehension when it fits on one readable line
Use generator expressions inside sum, max, any and all

p02.title: Sort by several things at once

beats.say: Sort trips by city A to Z, then by fare from highest to lowest, then by id. One line does it, if the key function returns a tuple.

Tuples compare item by item, so city decides first, then fare, then id. Putting a minus in front of the fare flips just that field to descending. For text you cannot negate, sort twice: by the second key first, then by the main key, because Python keeps equal items in their order.

items: Stable sort: sort twice for text

beats.say: And watch for this bug: xs equals xs dot sort sets xs to None, because sort works in place and returns nothing.

check.q: How do you sort by fare descending inside an otherwise ascending tuple key?
opts: Negate the fare in the key
check.why: reverse would flip every field; a minus flips only the fare.

work: Use a tuple key instead of chained sorts when the fields are numbers
Use sorted() when you need a new list; list.sort() returns None

p02.title: Decorators: wrap a function

beats.say: You want every pipeline step to log how long it took, without editing each step. A decorator does that.

show.sub: add behaviour without touching the function

beats.say: A decorator is a function that takes your function and returns a wrapper. The at sign line is just shorthand for f equals timed of f. The wrapper starts a clock, calls the original with whatever arguments it got, prints the time, and returns the result.
Always add functools wraps inside. Without it every decorated function is named wrapper in your logs and Airflow task names.

check.q: What does @timed above def f mean?
opts: timed runs once at import and is removed
check.why: The decorator replaces f with the wrapper it returns.

work: Add timing or logging to many steps with one decorator
Always use functools.wraps in your decorators

p02.title: Decorators with settings, like @retry(3)

beats.say: Retry three times sounds simple, but passing that number three makes the decorator one layer deeper than the timer we just built. Why?

Python first calls retry of three. That call must return the real decorator, which then takes your function and returns the wrapper that runs on every call. Three layers: settings, then the function, then each call.
You will meet this pattern all over: lru cache, Airflow task and dag, pytest fixtures and agent tools.

check.q: In @retry(3), what does retry(3) return?
opts: The decorator that takes the function
check.why: Settings first, then the decorator, then the wrapper.

work: Write retry as a decorator with settings and reuse it across API calls
Retry only transient errors, with backoff

p02.title: Pure functions make pipelines safe

beats.say: A nightly job fails halfway and you rerun it. Some rows are now cleaned twice and come out wrong. The cause is often one small habit: a cleaning function that changes its input.

A pure function returns a new value that depends only on its inputs, and changes nothing outside: no global updates, no editing the row you were given, no reading or writing files. Return a new dict instead of editing the old one.
Pure steps can be rerun safely, tested with a two-line assert, and run in parallel on many machines, which is exactly what Spark does. Keep the reading and writing at the edges.

check.q: Why do pure transformation steps make reruns safe?
opts: They change nothing outside, so running twice gives the same result
check.why: No hidden state changes means the second run sees the same inputs as the first.

work: Return new rows instead of mutating the ones passed in
Move file and database reads and writes to the start and end of a job

p03.title: Generators: functions that pause

beats.say: How do you process a 50 gigabyte file on a laptop with 8 gigabytes of memory? You never hold more than one record at a time. Generators make that easy.

A function with yield does not run when you call it. It returns a generator. Each time the loop asks for the next value, it runs until the next yield, hands back one value, and pauses right there, keeping its local variables.
So memory stays flat whatever the file size. The catch: a generator is used once. Loop over it a second time and you get nothing.

items: Lazy: one value at a time
Used once: second loop is empty

check.q: You loop over the same generator twice. What does the second loop see?
check.why: A generator is exhausted after one pass; make a new one or store a list if it is small.

work: Read big inputs with generators that yield parsed records
Never pass a generator to two consumers; create one per pass

p04.title: Composition over inheritance

beats.say: You have a CSV loader and a Parquet loader. Then someone needs Parquet with retries, and CSV from S3 with retries. With inheritance you end up with a class for every combination.

Inheritance says a thing is a kind of another thing, and it locks behaviour in at design time. Composition says a thing has parts: a loader holds a reader, a source and a retry policy, each a small object you can swap.
Three readers, three sources and two policies are eight small pieces, not eighteen classes. And each piece is easy to test alone.

check.q: Why does composition scale better than inheritance for loaders?
opts: Parts combine freely instead of needing a class per combination
check.why: You assemble behaviour from swappable parts rather than encoding every mix in a class tree.

work: Pass collaborators (reader, client, policy) into a class instead of subclassing
Use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship with shared behaviour

p05.title: Context managers: cleanup you cannot forget

beats.say: A job opens a database connection, fails halfway, and the connection stays open. Run it a hundred times and the database refuses new connections.

A with block guarantees the cleanup. Python calls enter at the start and exit at the end, and exit runs even when an exception flies out of the block. Files close, locks release, transactions roll back.
You can write your own with contextmanager: code before yield is the setup, code after yield, in a finally, is the cleanup.

check.q: An exception is raised inside a with block. Does the cleanup run?
opts: Only if you catch the exception
check.why: That guarantee is the reason to use with for every resource.

work: Open files, connections and locks only with "with"
Wrap temporary changes (env vars, working directory) in a small context manager

p06.title: Threads and the GIL

beats.say: You add eight threads to a CPU-heavy Python job and it gets no faster, sometimes slower. Yet eight threads make your API ingestion eight times faster. Why both?

Python has a global interpreter lock: only one thread runs Python code at a time. For computing, threads just take turns. But while a thread waits for the network or disk, it lets go of the lock, so other threads run.

items: One thread runs Python at a time
So threads help I/O, not CPU

beats.say: For CPU work, use processes, or libraries like NumPy that do the work outside Python.

check.q: Which job do threads speed up in standard Python?
opts: Parsing a large file in pure Python
Computing a big sum in a loop
check.why: Threads release the GIL while waiting on I/O.

work: Use a thread pool for API and database calls
Use a process pool or Spark for CPU-heavy transformations

r01.title: Migrations without drama

beats.say: Most platform migrations fail in the last ten percent: the few jobs nobody understands, which keep the old system alive for years.

Plan it like a product. Inventory every job and owner first. Migrate in waves, easiest first, to build the tooling. Run old and new side by side and compare outputs automatically, so each wave is proven, not promised.
And set a date when the old system becomes read-only. Without a deadline, the last ten percent never moves.

check.q: What usually stalls a big migration?
opts: The last few unowned, poorly understood jobs
check.why: Find owners early and set a read-only date for the old system.

work: Publish a migration dashboard: jobs moved, compared clean, retired
Agree a read-only date for the old platform with leadership

s00.title: The platform you will build

beats.say: Over this program you build one data platform for Meridian, a ride-hailing and food delivery company. Every module adds one layer while the rest keeps running.

show.sub: built a layer at a time

beats.say: Rider and driver apps send events to Kafka. Orders change in Postgres, and Debezium captures each change. Spark processes both, in batch and in streams, into Iceberg tables on object storage.
dbt turns those tables into clean models that Trino, Snowflake and Databricks serve to dashboards. Airflow schedules every step, and an on-call agent reads failures and reports them.

show.note: Airflow schedules it; an agent watches it

check.q: Which tool captures every change in the Postgres orders table?
check.why: Debezium reads the database log and turns each insert, update and delete into an event.

work: Draw your current platform in the same left-to-right way: sources, transport, processing, storage, serving
Mark which box has no owner or no monitoring

s00.sec: From a platform to a data foundation
s00.title: From a platform to a foundation

beats.say: A platform that one engineer runs is not yet a foundation a company can build on. Other teams need to use it without asking you every time.

show.sub: other teams use it without you

beats.say: Three things make the difference. Golden paths: a template that creates a new pipeline in minutes. Governance: every dataset has an owner, a class like personal or public, and a rule for who may read it and how long it is kept.
And the platform run as a product: onboarding, docs, published service levels, and showing each team what it costs. Modules O1 to O5 teach this.

check.q: What is a golden path?
opts: A ready-made template that sets up a new pipeline the approved way
check.why: It makes the right way the easy way: tests, logging and CI come with the template.

work: List what a new team must ask you before building a pipeline today: each item is a golden path to build
Give every important table a named owner

s01.title: Idempotency: the idea that connects everything

beats.say: Your nightly job failed at 3 a.m. Airflow retried it. Now yesterday's revenue is double. The retry did exactly what it was told.

A job is idempotent when running it twice leaves the same result as running it once. Appending is not: each run adds the rows again. Overwriting the day's partition is: the second run replaces the first.

show.unit: rows for 1 Nov after two runs

beats.say: Retries, backfills and replays all assume it. Overwrite partitions, or merge on a key, never blind append.

check.q: Which write makes a daily job safe to rerun?
check.why: The second run replaces the first instead of adding to it.

work: Check every scheduled job: what happens if it runs twice?
Write by partition overwrite or merge on a key

s02.title: Iceberg: a table is a tree of metadata

beats.say: Two jobs write the same lake table at once and a reader sees half of each. Plain Parquet folders cannot stop that. Iceberg can, without a database server.

show.sub: what readers see on plain folders

beats.say: An Iceberg table is a tree. The catalog points at the current metadata file. That lists snapshots, each snapshot lists manifest files, and manifests list the data files with their column statistics.

A commit writes new files, then swaps the catalog pointer in one atomic step. Readers see the old snapshot or the new one, never half. Old snapshots give time travel, and statistics let queries skip files.

check.q: What makes an Iceberg commit atomic?
opts: A lock on every data file
Swapping the catalog's pointer to a new metadata file in one step
check.why: Everything else is written first; the commit is a single pointer change.

work: Expire old snapshots and compact small files on a schedule
Use a catalog that supports atomic swaps (REST, Glue, Nessie)

s03.title: The shuffle: where Spark jobs get slow

beats.say: Your Spark job reads a terabyte in two minutes, then spends forty minutes on one group by. That forty minutes is the shuffle.

To group by city, every row for Pune must end up on the same executor. So each task writes its rows to local disk, split by key, and then every task fetches its piece from every other machine over the network. That is disk, network and sorting, all at once.
Shuffle less: filter and select columns first, broadcast small tables, and partition on the join key.

items: Avoid repeated shuffles on the same key

check.q: Why is a shuffle expensive?
opts: Data is written to disk and sent over the network between executors
check.why: Every task exchanges data with every other task.

work: Read the plan for Exchange steps and ask whether each is needed
Broadcast dimension tables under a few hundred megabytes

s04.title: Late data and backfills

beats.say: Yesterday's revenue report is published at 6 a.m. At 9 a.m., two thousand trips from a phone that was offline arrive, all dated yesterday. Is the report now wrong?

Yes, unless the pipeline expects it. Partition by event date, not load date, and reprocess the last few days each night, so late rows land in the right day. Mark days as final only after the lateness window passes.
A backfill is the same job pointed at older dates. If every step overwrites its partition, a backfill is safe to run any time.

check.q: Where should late-arriving trips land?
opts: In today's partition, the load date
In the partition of their event date
In a separate late table forever
check.why: Event-date partitions plus a lookback window keep each day's numbers right.

work: Measure how late your data really arrives and set the lookback to cover it
Publish a "final" flag per day for finance

s05.title: Why Kafka is fast: the diary version

beats.say: Imagine keeping a diary. Do you open it to a random page each time, or just write on the next empty line? The next line, of course. No flipping, no searching. Kafka writes its data exactly like that.

show.title: Why is Kafka *fast*? The diary version

cells.label: a diary: always the next empty line

beats.say: Now picture shelving books where every new book must go on a different shelf across the building. You would spend the day walking, not shelving. A hard disk does that walking when writes are scattered: a small arm moves to each spot.

nodes.label: Hard disk
nodes.sub: the arm walks to each spot

chip.text: Time goes to moving, not writing

beats.say: Kafka keeps one diary per stream of events and only ever adds to the end, so the disk keeps writing without walking around. That is the first reason it can take in so much data.

check.q: In the diary picture, why is writing fast?
opts: You always write on the next empty line
check.why: Always writing at the end means no jumping around: on a disk, no arm movement.

work: Explain Kafka to non-engineers with the diary picture: it only ever adds to the end
Remember the reason: it never jumps around, not that it skips the disk

s05.title: Kafka writes to disk. Why is it fast?

beats.say: Kafka saves every message to disk, and disks are supposed to be slow. Yet one broker takes in hundreds of megabytes a second. How?

show.kicker: Asked in almost every streaming round
show.title: Kafka writes everything to disk. So why is it *fast*?

beats.say: First, what makes a disk slow. A hard disk has an arm that must physically move to the place where data goes. That move is a seek, about ten milliseconds. Writes scattered all over the disk spend their time moving the arm, not writing.

chip.text: Each move of the arm is a *seek*: about 10 ms

beats.say: Kafka never writes in scattered places. A partition is one file, and each new message goes at the end, right after the last one. The arm stays put and data streams down in one run: over a hundred megabytes a second instead of under one.

cells.label: partition 0 · one file · new messages go at the end

check.q: Why does appending to the end of a log make Kafka's disk writes fast?
opts: The disk does not have to move to a new place between writes
Kafka finds each message with an index
check.why: No seek between writes: the data goes down in one continuous run. It is about not moving, not about searching. SSDs have no arm, but they also prefer large sequential writes.

work: Size Kafka disks for sequential bandwidth (MB/s), not random operations per second
Keep other busy random-write workloads off the brokers' log disks
Prefer fewer, larger partitions per disk over thousands of tiny ones

s05.title: Kafka is fast: page cache, zero-copy, batching

beats.say: Second trick: Kafka does not keep its own cache. It writes into the page cache, the part of memory where the operating system keeps recent file data. Consumers that keep up read new messages straight from that memory, so most reads never touch the disk.
Third: zero-copy. To send messages, Kafka asks the operating system to move bytes from the page cache straight to the network card, without copying them through Kafka's own memory.
Fourth: batching. Producers send many messages in one compressed request, so one write and one network trip carry thousands of messages. Spread partitions over brokers and it all runs in parallel.

chip.text: Partitions on many brokers run *in parallel*

check.q: A consumer is keeping up with the newest messages. Where do its reads mostly come from?
opts: A disk seek for every message
The operating system's page cache in memory
check.why: Recent data is still in the page cache, so it is served from memory. A consumer far behind reads old data from disk and is slower: another reason to watch consumer lag.

work: Leave most broker RAM to the OS page cache; keep the Java heap modest
Turn on producer batching and compression: linger.ms, batch.size, compression.type
Alert on consumer lag: a lagging consumer reads from disk and falls further behind

s05.title: Kafka speed: when it matters, and what it costs

beats.say: So Kafka is fast. As an architect, the real questions are different: when does that speed stop being the limit, and what does running it cost you?

Broker speed is rarely the limit. Partitions are. They cap how many consumers can work in parallel, and order holds only inside one partition. Too few and reads cannot scale; too many and rebalances, open files and leader elections slow everything down.

chip.text: Too many: slow rebalances and elections

beats.say: Cost is storage and operations: throughput times retention times three replicas. Fifty megabytes a second kept for seven days is about ninety terabytes. At two hundred events a minute, a managed queue or a plain table is cheaper.

chip.text: Low volume? A *managed queue* or a table

check.q: What usually limits Kafka at scale before raw broker speed?
check.why: Partitions decide parallelism and ordering; get them wrong and no broker speed helps.

work: Size partitions from target consumer parallelism and peak throughput
Estimate storage as throughput × retention × replicas before choosing Kafka
Prefer managed Kafka or a simpler queue for low volume

s05.title: Exactly once is really at least once plus

beats.say: Kafka promises exactly once. Yet your sink table has duplicates after a crash. Both statements can be true.
A consumer reads, writes to the sink, then commits its offset. If it crashes after writing but before committing, it restarts from the old offset and writes those rows again. That is at least once.

Exactly once in effect needs the sink to cooperate: either commit output and offsets together in one transaction, or make writes idempotent with a merge on the event id. Then a replay changes nothing.

chip.text: Commit output *and* offsets in one transaction
Or make writes idempotent: *MERGE* on event_id

check.q: A consumer crashes after writing but before committing offsets. What happens on restart?
opts: Those records are processed and written again
check.why: It resumes from the last committed offset, so the sink must handle repeats.

work: Give every event a unique id and merge on it in the sink
Store offsets in the same transaction as the output where the sink allows

s06.title: Log-based change capture

beats.say: Your nightly job copies orders where updated at is after yesterday. It misses deleted orders, and rows updated twice in a day show only once. The database already keeps a perfect record of every change.

Every database writes each change to its log before applying it, for crash recovery. Debezium reads that log, the write ahead log in Postgres or the binlog in MySQL, and turns every insert, update and delete into an event, in commit order.
No extra load on the tables, no missed deletes, and every change in order. Debezium remembers its log position, so after a restart it carries on where it stopped.

check.q: Why does log-based CDC catch deletes when an updated_at query does not?
opts: Deletes are written to the database log like any other change
check.why: A deleted row is gone from the table but its delete is in the log.

work: Prefer log-based CDC over timestamp queries for tables with deletes
Monitor replication slot lag so the database log does not fill the disk

s07.title: IAM: who may do what to which bucket

beats.say: An analytics job only needs to read one folder in S3. It was given admin access because that worked. A leaked key from that job can now delete every bucket.

In AWS every request is checked against policies: which principal, which action, on which resource. Deny wins, otherwise an explicit allow is needed. A role is an identity a service assumes for short-lived keys, so nothing long-lived sits in code.
Least privilege means the job gets get object on that one prefix, nothing more, and its role expires its keys automatically.

check.q: Which grants least privilege to a job that reads trips data?
check.why: Only the action and the prefix the job needs.

work: Replace long-lived access keys with roles
Use access analyzer to find unused permissions and remove them

s08.title: Delta Lake: a table is its transaction log

beats.say: A Delta table looks like a folder of Parquet files. But reading the files directly gives wrong answers: deleted rows come back. The truth is in a folder called delta log.

Every commit adds a numbered JSON file to the log, listing the data files it added and removed. To read version 12, Delta replays the log up to 12. Every ten commits it writes a Parquet checkpoint so readers do not replay thousands of files.
Two writers race to create the same next number; only one succeeds. The other checks for conflicts and retries.

check.q: How does a Delta reader know which files make up the current table?
opts: It replays the transaction log from the last checkpoint
check.why: Files on disk may be removed or uncommitted; only the log says what counts.

work: Never read Delta tables as plain Parquet folders
Run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM on a schedule with retention you agree with the business

s09.title: Write, audit, publish

beats.say: A bad load wrote negative fares into the revenue table at 2 a.m. By 9 a.m. three dashboards and a finance export had used them.

Write, audit, publish stops that. The job writes to a staging branch or table that nobody reads. Checks run there: row counts, nulls, ranges, uniqueness. Only if they pass does the job publish, by swapping the new data in at once.
With Iceberg branches or a table swap, publishing is one atomic step, so readers never see half-checked data.

check.q: Where do the checks run in write, audit, publish?
opts: On the published table after readers use it
On a staging copy before it is published
check.why: Auditing before publishing is the whole point.

work: Add a staging step and checks before your most-read tables are updated
Alert and keep yesterday's data when an audit fails

s10.title: Capacity arithmetic in two minutes

beats.say: In a design round the interviewer says: ten million riders, design the trip events pipeline. Before boxes and arrows, they want numbers.

show.sub: what does that mean per second?

beats.say: Say it out loud: ten million riders, two trips a day, fifty events per trip, is a billion events a day. A day has about a hundred thousand seconds, so ten thousand events a second on average, maybe thirty thousand at peak. At one kilobyte each, a terabyte a day.
Those numbers choose the design: partitions, storage, and whether one machine is enough.

check.q: Roughly how many seconds are in a day, for quick estimates?
check.why: 86,400, rounded to a hundred thousand for mental maths.

work: Do the arithmetic before drawing any design
Plan for peak, usually 2 to 5 times the average

s11.title: Experiments: was it the feature or the week?

beats.say: Bookings rose eight percent the week the new home screen shipped. The product manager wants to celebrate. It was also the start of the festival season.

A before and after comparison cannot separate the two. An experiment can: randomly show the new screen to half the users at the same time. The festival hits both halves equally, so the difference between them is the feature.
Decide the metric and the sample size before starting, and do not stop the moment it looks good; early peeks make noise look like wins.

check.q: Why does a randomised split answer the question when before-and-after cannot?
opts: Both groups share the same week, so outside effects cancel
check.why: Randomisation balances everything except the change you made.

work: Ask for a control group before claiming a feature moved a metric
Write down the metric and stopping rule before the test starts

s12.title: Order your interviews

beats.say: You have six companies to interview with and one dream company. Most people book the dream company first, while they are least practised.

Interviewing is a skill that improves with each loop. Start with two companies you would accept but care less about, then the mid group, and put your top choices in the same two weeks at the end, when you are sharpest.
Grouping the final ones together also means offers arrive together, which gives you options and leverage when you negotiate.

check.q: Why cluster your top-choice interviews at the end?
opts: You are most practised then, and offers arrive together
check.why: Peak skill and parallel offers both help.

work: List your companies in three tiers and book the lowest tier first
Ask recruiters for timelines so your final offers land in the same week
